title: Terraform and GitHub Automation with Claude
tagline: Terraform step by step, the mistakes that burn teams, and a GitHub workflow where Claude reviews and a human approves
audience: Enterprise IT and network operations teams, load balancer and data center engineers, platform and DevOps teams adopting infrastructure as code
prerequisites: Basic Linux command line and text editing
Basic networking and load balancer concepts (VIP, pool, certificate)
Git basics are helpful, not required
No prior Terraform or Python experience required
outcomes: Write, plan and apply Terraform configurations step by step with providers, variables, modules, remote state and locking
Recognise and fix the common Terraform mistakes: unpinned providers, secrets in code, state in Git, count versus for_each, targeted applies and drift
Run a GitHub repository for infrastructure code with branches, pull requests, CODEOWNERS, branch protection and GitHub Actions plan-on-PR and apply-on-merge
Set up Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK and an MCP server so Claude can draft, plan and review Terraform without ever running apply itself
Build a plan-review agent that reads terraform show -json output and posts a structured risk verdict to the pull request
Enforce guardrails, environment approvals and an audit trail for every plan and apply across F5, NetScaler, Cisco ACI and other load balancers (Anaya LB)

modules.title: Infrastructure as code for network and load balancer teams
topics: Why Terraform for F5, NetScaler, Cisco ACI and cloud: declarative config versus click-ops and ad hoc scripts
HCL building blocks: providers, resources, data sources, variables, outputs and the state file
The course pattern: Claude plans and explains, Terraform and pipelines execute, a human approves, everything is logged
Lab environment tour: GitHub organization, lab F5 and NetScaler, Cisco ACI simulator, Terraform CLI on Linux
modules.lab: Install Terraform, clone the course repository and run terraform init and plan against a sample F5 BIG-IP pool configuration.
modules.deliverable: Working Terraform workstation and first successful plan.

modules.title: Setting up Claude Code, the Agent SDK and MCP for Terraform work
topics: Claude Code in the repository: CLAUDE.md conventions, allowed commands, and why apply is never on the allowed list
Claude Agent SDK basics in Python: a session, tool use, structured JSON output with a schema
An MCP server that exposes terraform fmt, validate, plan and show -json as read-only tools
Prompting Claude to explain a plan in plain English and cite the resource addresses it refers to
modules.lab: Configure Claude Code for the repo, start the Terraform MCP server, and ask Claude to explain a plan without being able to apply it.
modules.deliverable: Claude Code plus MCP setup with a read-only Terraform tool set.

modules.title: Terraform scripting step by step: init, plan, apply, state
topics: The lifecycle: init, fmt, validate, plan, apply, destroy; reading a plan symbol by symbol (+, -, ~, -/+)
Variables, tfvars files, locals, outputs and the first reusable module for an F5 virtual server and pool
terraform import for a virtual server that already exists; terraform state list, show, mv and rm
Remote state with locking, workspaces for dev and prod, and pinned provider versions in required_providers
modules.lab: Build a module for an F5 virtual server with Claude drafting the HCL, import an existing pool, and move state to a locked remote backend.
modules.deliverable: Reusable virtual server module with remote, locked state.

modules.title: Common Terraform mistakes and how to catch them early
topics: Unpinned provider versions, secrets hard coded in variables, and the .tfstate file committed to Git
count versus for_each, resource recreation from a renamed block, and the moved block as the fix
Drift left behind by terraform apply -target, manual changes on the device, and detecting drift with plan -detailed-exitcode
Wiring the catchers: terraform fmt -check, validate, tflint, a pre-commit hook and a Claude review that names the mistake and the line
modules.lab: Reproduce five classic mistakes in the lab repo, watch each one surface in plan or review, and fix them one by one.
modules.deliverable: Mistake catalogue with reproduction and fix for each, plus pre-commit checks.

modules.title: GitHub repository fundamentals for infrastructure code
topics: Repository layout for Terraform: environments, modules, .gitignore for state, plans and credentials
Branches, commits, pull requests, reviews and merge strategies for a network team
CODEOWNERS, branch protection rules, required reviewers and status checks
Secrets and variables in GitHub: repository secrets, environment secrets, OIDC to cloud and Vault, and short-lived device credentials fetched at run time
modules.lab: Create the team repository, protect main, add CODEOWNERS for the F5 and ACI folders, and raise your first pull request from a feature branch.
modules.deliverable: Protected GitHub repository with pull request workflow.

modules.title: GitHub Actions pipelines: plan on pull request, apply on merge
topics: Workflow anatomy: triggers, jobs, hashicorp/setup-terraform, caching and concurrency groups to avoid parallel applies
Plan on every pull request with the plan output posted as a PR comment; fmt, validate and tflint as required checks
Apply only on merge to main, scoped to a GitHub environment with required reviewers
Saving the plan file as an artifact so the apply uses exactly the plan that was reviewed
modules.lab: Write the plan and apply workflows with Claude Code, open a pull request, read the plan comment and merge to see the gated apply run.

modules.title: Guardrails, approvals and audit for Terraform and GitHub automation
topics: Policy checks before apply: allowed resource types, no destroy without a linked change ticket, no changes outside the PR scope
GitHub environment protection rules and required reviewers as the human approval gate for every apply
Audit record per change: who asked, what Claude recommended, plan hash, approver, apply result and run URL
Least privilege for pipelines and agents: read-only device accounts for plan, scoped tokens, no long-lived credentials in the pipeline
modules.lab: Add a policy job that blocks a destroy without a ticket, require approval on the prod environment, and export the audit record for one change.
modules.deliverable: Guardrail policy, approval gate and audit record format.

modules.title: Claude as plan reviewer: Agent SDK, MCP and structured verdicts
topics: An Agent SDK application that reads terraform show -json and returns risk level, affected resources and a summary in a fixed JSON schema
Posting the verdict as a pull request comment and as a check run through the GitHub API; the agent never merges or applies
Prompt and schema tests: deletes, replacements, certificate changes and out-of-scope resources must be flagged correctly
Handling uncertainty: the agent marks unknowns and asks for a human when the plan touches resources it cannot classify
modules.lab: Build and test the plan-review agent, run it inside the pull request workflow and watch it flag a hidden resource replacement.
modules.deliverable: Plan-review agent with schema tests wired into the PR pipeline.

modules.title: Terraform for F5, NetScaler, Cisco ACI and other load balancers
topics: F5 BIG-IP provider: bigip_ltm_node, bigip_ltm_pool, bigip_ltm_virtual_server and bigip_ssl_certificate backed by iControl REST
Citrix ADC provider for NetScaler: citrixadc_lbvserver, citrixadc_servicegroup and bindings over the NITRO API
Cisco ACI provider: aci_tenant, aci_application_profile, aci_bridge_domain against the APIC REST API
Where no provider exists: Python wrappers for Radware Alteon and other load balancers (Anaya LB) driven from the same pipeline with the same approval gate
modules.lab: Add a NetScaler virtual server and an ACI bridge domain through the pull request workflow, and attach a Python-driven Radware change to the same gate.
modules.deliverable: Multi-platform Terraform modules behind one approval workflow.

modules.title: Capstone: end-to-end change through the Claude-reviewed pipeline
topics: A change request in, a reviewed pull request, a Claude verdict, a human approval, a gated apply and an audit record out
Runbook: how to raise, review, approve, apply and revert a change in this repository
Handover: CODEOWNERS, environment reviewers and audit export for the team
Acceptance review: mistakes caught, approvals enforced, rollback by reverting the pull request, demo to the group
modules.deliverable: End-to-end Terraform and GitHub workflow with Claude review and runbook.

narration: hook
Your Terraform apply just removed a production virtual server. The plan said minus one. Nobody read it. The change went through at two in the morning, and the incident bridge opened at six.
hook

What if Claude read every plan, explained every change in plain English, flagged the common mistakes before they reached a device, and the apply ran only after a person clicked approve? That is Terraform and GitHub automation, done with Claude, done safely.
intro
Gennoor Tech presents Terraform and GitHub Automation with Claude.
story

One repository. One pull request per change. You learn Terraform step by step, you learn the mistakes that burn real teams, and you put Claude to work as planner, explainer and reviewer. Claude drafts the code and reads the plan. Deterministic pipelines run the apply. A human approves anything that touches a device, and every step is logged. By the end you own a repository your whole team can work in.
path0

You start with infrastructure as code for network and load balancer teams. Providers, resources, variables, outputs and state, written in H C L. Then you set up Claude Code, the Claude Agent S D K and an M C P server that exposes the Terraform C L I as tools, so the agent can run init, validate and plan, but never apply on its own. You will see exactly which tools the agent holds and which it does not.
path0

Then Terraform, step by step. Init, plan, apply, and the state file that makes it all work. You read a plan line by line, you import a virtual server that already exists, and you move to remote state with locking, workspaces for dev and prod, and modules you can reuse for every site.
path1

Day two opens with the common mistakes. Unpinned provider versions. Secrets hard coded in variables. Count where for each belonged. A state file committed to Git. A targeted apply that left drift behind. Each mistake gets a name, a symptom and a fix. You reproduce each one in the lab, then wire in the checks that catch it: terraform format, validate, tflint and a Claude review that names the mistake and cites the line.
path2

Then GitHub. Branches, commits, a git ignore that keeps state and secrets out of the repository, pull requests with required reviewers, code owners and branch protection. GitHub Actions runs plan on every pull request and apply only on merge, with the plan output posted as a comment for the team to read before anyone clicks approve. Guardrails follow: an allow list of resource types, a block on destroy without a change ticket, approval gates in GitHub environments, and an audit record for every plan and apply.
path3

Day three brings the agent into the review loop. An Agent S D K application reads the plan as J S O N, returns a structured verdict with risk level, affected resources and a plain English summary, and posts it to the pull request. It never merges and it never applies. When it cannot classify a resource, it says so and asks for a human.
path3

Finally, the devices themselves. The F5 BIG-IP provider for virtual servers, pools and certificates. The Citrix A D C provider for NetScaler. The Cisco A C I provider for tenants and bridge domains. And Python wrappers for Radware Alteon and other load balancers (Anaya LB) where no provider exists, so one workflow covers the whole estate.
labs

Every lab runs against a shared GitHub organization and lab devices in a sandbox. Nothing you do in the lab can reach a production device. You will commit a state file on purpose, watch Claude catch it, break a plan with an unintended destroy, and see the approval gate hold until a person says yes.
stats
Ten modules. Three days, hands-on. Five common mistakes reproduced and fixed. And zero applies without a human approval.
who

This course is for enterprise I T and network operations teams, load balancer and data center engineers, and platform teams moving to infrastructure as code, in India and worldwide. You need basic Linux and networking knowledge. Git helps, and no prior Terraform is required.
